newsitem.title: USA: New Burger King chief eyes international market.
newsitem.headline: New Burger King chief eyes international market.

text.p: Fast food operator Burger King Corp. named a new chief executive Thursday, and he indicated the company would focus on increasing its share of the international market for quick restaurant food.
Britain's Grand Metropolitan Plc, which owns Burger King, appointed Dennis Malamatinas to replace Robert Lowes, whose departure was "a mutual decision," the company said.
Burger King's hamburger restaurants compete fiercely with McDonald's Corp. in the United States, but Malamatinas noted that only about 20 percent of Burger King's sales come outside of North America.
"That's my primary job, my primary focus ... We'd like to increase that," he said in a telephone interview.
Industry analysts said they were surprised at the timing of the announcement, which they said seemed sudden.

Burger King, the second-largest U.S. fast food chain after McDonald's, has been gaining ground on its larger rival. Burger King's share of the U.S. quick-serve hamburger market rose to 19.2 percent last year from 18.2 percent a year earlier, while McDonald's slipped 0.2 percentage point to 42.1 percent.
"He (Lowes) must have had political problems with someone," said one financial analyst who asked not to be identified by name.

Charles Anderson, corporate relations director at Grand Metropolitan, said of the timing only that Malamatinas and Paul Clayton, who was promoted to president of Burger King North America from senior vice president of worldwide marketing, were a strong, dynamic team in a changing industry.
"This is a dynamic business where there is a great deal of change," he said.
Grand Met also said that John McGrath, group chief executive, also would assume the duties of chairman of Burger King Corp.

Malamatinas said he viewed growth in Europe as the No. 1 international opportunity, followed by the Asia/Pacific and Latin American markets. "Somehow, we'll have to learn how to move even faster, more aggressively," he said.
Malamatinas, 41, was most recently executive director and president of Grand Met's International Distillers and Vintners, Asia Pacific, the company's drinks business in Hong Kong.
Overall, observers said they expected the appointment would be a positive.

"Obviously, he's got a lot of international experience. He's been in the food and beverage business for a long time. It looks like he's got a pretty good handle on the business," said Dean Haskell at Everens Securities in Chicago.
"He looks like a guy that will continue to keep Burger King focused on the fundamentals of the business, which I think is a very important aspect of their business strategy," he said.
Malamatinas said Burger King was in a strong position.
"I think the company is in great shape. It is probably in the best shape it's been during its history," he said.
"We will be basically providing a dual focus on the business," Malamatinas said of himself and Clayton, 38.
Malamatinas declined to make specific growth projections or to discuss price-cutting in the hamburger business, recently initiated by McDonald's.

Several industry analysts have said recently that fast-food chicken restaurant chains, notably Boston Chicken Inc., could be the fiercest competitors for Burger King, McDonald's and other hamburger chains.
